hints: Think about which single large vessel leaves the left ventricle to supply oxygenated blood to all body organs, from which smaller arteries branch off.
walkthrough:
Trace Blood From The Heart**
All oxygenated blood leaving the heart for the body exits through the left ventricle into one very large elastic artery. Every other systemic artery, including the hepatic artery to the liver, is ultimately a branch of this vessel.

Name The Vessel**
That main artery is the aorta. Spelling must be correct to gain the mark.

hints: Look at Fig. 3.1 and focus on what lies between blood in the sinusoid and the hepatocytes, and what the labelled gaps remove as a barrier.
walkthrough:
See The Barrier That Is Missing**
In a normal capillary, endothelial cells form a continuous wall so substances must cross through or between tightly joined cells. In Fig. 3.1 the sinusoid wall has large gaps between endothelial cells, so plasma has direct access to the space around hepatocytes.

Link Structure To Exchange**
This means nutrients, plasma proteins and other large molecules can move quickly between blood and hepatocytes without crossing a cell layer. Kupffer cells can also move through. Any one valid advantage linked to easier movement or exchange gains the mark.
Final answer: Large gaps allow easier / faster exchange of substances between blood / sinusoid and hepatocytes / tissue fluid, as substances do not have to cross an endothelial cell layer.

hints: Recall the general type of bulk uptake used by an immune phagocyte to take in a whole cell like a red blood cell.
Picture how the cell surface membrane changes shape to surround the target cell completely.
Think about what membrane-bound sac now holds the red blood cell inside the Kupffer cell, and which organelle must join it.
Remember what type of enzymes that organelle provides and what useful products result from digesting haemoglobin.
walkthrough:
Engulf The Red Blood Cell**
The Kupffer cell carries out phagocytosis, a form of endocytosis. Its cell surface membrane extends pseudopodia that surround and envelop the damaged red blood cell.

Trap It In A Vacuole**
When the membrane fuses around the cell, the red blood cell is internalised in a phagocytic vacuole called a phagosome, separate from the cytoplasm.

Add Digestive Enzymes**
A lysosome then fuses with the phagosome. Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes such as proteases that work to break down large molecules.

Digest And Recycle**
The enzymes digest the red blood cell contents, breaking haemoglobin down to haem and globin / amino acids, which can then be recycled or excreted.

Final answer: Phagocytosis / endocytosis; red blood cell engulfed by pseudopodia to form phagosome / phagocytic vacuole; lysosome fuses with phagosome; hydrolytic / digestive enzymes digest haemoglobin to haem and globin / amino acids.

hints: Start with the list of hepatocyte functions at the top of the question and match each one to a structure you can see in Fig. 3.2.
Look for membrane systems with and without small dark dots, and for large organelles with internal membranes that supply energy for these demanding synthetic jobs.
Use the already labelled glycogen granules and lipid droplet as clues to energy storage, and think what synthesis roles the unlabelled membranes must have.
walkthrough:
Link Lipid Synthesis To Smooth Membranes**
Hepatocytes synthesise triglycerides and cholesterol. The network of tubular membranes without ribosomes in Fig. 3.2 is smooth endoplasmic reticulum, the site of lipid synthesis. Label it.

Link Protein Synthesis To Rough Membranes**
Hepatocytes synthesise plasma proteins. The flattened sacs studded with ribosomes are rough endoplasmic reticulum, the site of protein synthesis. Label it.

Explain Energy Supply And Storage**
These syntheses plus detoxification need large amounts of ATP, so many mitochondria for aerobic respiration are visible. The labelled glycogen granules store glucose and the labelled lipid droplet stores lipid / fatty acids for energy. Any three such evidence points with correct labels gain full marks.

Final answer: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum for triglyceride / lipid / cholesterol synthesis; rough endoplasmic reticulum with ribosomes for plasma protein / enzyme synthesis; many mitochondria for aerobic respiration to provide ATP; glycogen granules as glucose store; lipid droplet as energy / fatty acid store. Labels added to Fig. 3.2.

hints: Compare the boundary and the inside of the labelled peroxisome with the larger organelles in Fig. 3.2, looking closely at number of membranes and internal folds.
walkthrough:
Compare Membranes And Interiors**
Look carefully at Fig. 3.2. The peroxisome is a dense spherical body with a single limiting membrane and a uniform interior. The mitochondria are larger, bounded by two membranes and contain internal folds called cristae. Stating either the double membrane, presence of cristae, or shape difference is enough.
Final answer: Mitochondrion has a double membrane / cristae whereas peroxisome has a single membrane and no cristae; or mitochondria show varied / elongated shapes whereas peroxisome is spherical.

hints: Think about what information and machinery any organelle needs in order to make its own proteins from scratch.
Recall which of these two organelles retains remnants of its own genetic system and ability to make ATP, and which must import all its proteins.
walkthrough:
What Mitochondria Still Possess**
Mitochondria contain their own small circular DNA with genes for some mitochondrial enzymes, plus 70S ribosomes and the enzymes for transcription and translation. They also generate ATP to power protein synthesis.

Why Peroxisomes Cannot**
Peroxisomes have no DNA and no ribosomes, so they have no instructions and no site for assembling amino acids into enzymes. All peroxisomal enzymes like catalase must be coded by nuclear DNA, made on cytoplasmic ribosomes and imported.

Final answer: Mitochondrion has DNA / genes coding for enzymes and 70S ribosomes / transcription-translation enzymes plus ATP supply for synthesis; peroxisome has no DNA / ribosomes so cannot synthesise enzymes.

hints: Think about the danger if a toxic intermediate like hydrogen peroxide were allowed to diffuse freely through the cytoplasm.
Consider how keeping catalase and its substrate together inside a small membrane-bound space affects safety and speed of breakdown.
walkthrough:
Protect The Cell By Isolation**
Hydrogen peroxide is toxic and can damage proteins, membranes and DNA. Enclosing catalase with its substrate inside the peroxisome membrane prevents hydrogen peroxide from contacting the rest of the cytoplasm.

Speed Up The Reaction**
The compartment also holds a high concentration of catalase in one place, so more enzyme-substrate complexes form and breakdown is fast and controlled under optimum conditions. The harmless oxygen produced can then be used in other peroxisome or mitochondrial reactions.

Final answer: Membrane keeps toxic hydrogen peroxide isolated so rest of cell is protected; compartment concentrates enzyme and substrate for more efficient breakdown / provides optimum conditions; oxygen released can be used for other reactions.
